text: If the Iliad is a poem about rage, the Odyssey is a poem about a journey home — the longest, hardest homecoming ever told.
It begins not with a goddess, and not with wrath, but with a man. In the original Greek, ἄνδρα — a man of many turns, many troubles, many disguises.
The poem is the Odyssey. Its hero is Odysseus, who fought ten years at Troy, and would wander ten years more before he reached his home.
Here is how it opens, in Homer's own Greek: Ἄνδρα μοι ἔννεπε, Μοῦσα, πολύτροπον.
In English, it asks the Muse: tell me of the man of many turns, the man of twists and wiles.
The very first word is ἄνδρα — the man. Not yet his name. First we are told only that he is πολύτροπος, the man of many ways, of many turnings.
He saw the cities of many people and came to know their minds. And on the open sea he suffered sorrow after sorrow, fighting for his own life and the homecoming of his men.
But he could not save them. They perished by their own reckless folly — fools, who devoured the cattle of the Sun, and the god took from them the day of their return.
And now, far from home, Odysseus is held on a lonely island by the nymph Calypso, longing only to see the smoke rising from his own land of Ithaca.
And so begins the Odyssey, the long and wandering journey of Odysseus, the man of many turns, as he struggles year after year to find his way home.
